summary: KS3 learners (ages 11-13) construct and interpret the full family of statistical displays — frequency tables (including GROUPED tables for continuous/large numerical data), bar charts, pie charts, pictograms and vertical line charts — and crucially CHOOSE the representation that fits the data type. Two ideas do the teaching work. First, grouping continuous data demands class intervals that are non-overlapping and gap-free, so every value falls in exactly one class — which is why inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) matters, to fix where a boundary value goes; equal class widths are the usual KS3 choice so that bar heights can be compared fairly, but equal widths are not what puts each value in exactly one class. Second, the representation must match the data: categorical data suits bar charts, pie charts or pictograms; ungrouped discrete numerical data suits a vertical line chart; grouped continuous data suits touching bars/histograms; proportions of a whole suit a pie chart; genuine time-series data suits a line graph. Because this skill is representational, understanding shows in CONSTRUCTING a display, not just reading one.
misconceptions: Choosing overlapping or ambiguous class intervals (0-10, 10-20) so a boundary value could go in either class, or leaving gaps that omit values
Choosing a representation that doesn't fit the data type — e.g. a line graph joining categorical bars, or a pie chart where the whole is not meaningful
Calculating pie-chart angles by dividing 360° by the frequency instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total
Miscounting raw data into the table (helped by tallying), or reading a single value from a comparative chart instead of concluding about the difference

activities.title: Grouped-table-and-chart workshop (set intervals, then choose a chart)
steps: Take a strip of raw running times (e.g. 30 runners' times to the nearest second) and set your own class-interval boundaries so the intervals are equal, non-overlapping and gap-free and cover the whole range.
Place each raw value into exactly one class; deliberately try writing intervals as 0-10 and 10-20, then find where a runner who took exactly 10 seconds goes — notice the ambiguity.
Rewrite the intervals using inequality notation (0≤t<10, 10≤t<20…) and confirm the boundary value now has exactly one home.
Choose which chart suits this data — bar chart, pie chart, line graph or histogram-style touching bars — then draw it and check the drawing against the data type.
If you choose a pie chart, compute each sector angle as (frequency ÷ total) × 360° and check the angles sum to 360°.
activities.insight: Boundary ambiguity is resolved by inequality notation so every value belongs to exactly one class; and the chart must match the data type — a line joining categorical bars implies an order and continuous change between categories that do not exist, whereas grouped continuous data is shown with touching bars (a frequency polygon through class midpoints is a separate, legitimate display for grouped continuous data).

activities.title: Count raw data into a frequency table with tallies
steps: Take a set of raw data (e.g. favourite sports of a class, or heights measured to the nearest cm) and count each value into its row using tally marks.
Convert the tallies to frequencies and check the frequencies sum to the total number of data points.
For continuous or wide-ranging numerical data, group into equal class intervals in inequality notation before tallying.
activities.insight: Tallying keeps counting accurate and reliable; frequencies should reconcile with the total, catching miscounts.

activities.title: Which chart fits? Decide, justify, and interpret comparatively
steps: Sort several data sets by which display suits them: categorical → bar chart or pie chart; grouped continuous → touching bars/histogram; proportions of a whole → pie chart; genuine time-series → line graph.
For a categorical case (e.g. pupils' favourite sports), decide whether a line graph would be a good choice and explain why or why not.
Read a bar chart comparing Class A and Class B and state a CONCLUSION about the difference between the two data sets, citing both, not just one bar's value.
Given a grouped frequency table, name the modal class (the interval with the highest frequency).
activities.insight: Choosing a display is a judgement driven by data type, and interpreting a comparative chart means concluding about the difference between data sets, not reading a single value.

activities.title: Annotated reference: contrast displays side by side
steps: Study a bar chart of categorical data (bars with gaps) set beside a histogram-style display of grouped continuous data (bars touching) and note what each tells you about the data type.
Examine a grouped frequency table in inequality notation and identify how the boundary value is assigned.
Reveal, for each chart type, which data type it suits and add that to a 'which chart?' decision aid.
activities.insight: The touching-versus-gapped bars distinction signals continuous versus categorical data; the notation shows where boundary values belong.

checkQuestion: Two moves. FIRST, interpret given representations: (a) 'Here is a grouped frequency table of pupils' heights — which is the modal class?' (b) 'This bar chart compares Class A and Class B's scores — what can you conclude about the difference?' THEN, translate/construct: 'Here is the raw data — the times, to the nearest second, of 30 runners. Make a grouped frequency table (choose your own class intervals), then decide the best chart to display it and draw it.' Watch especially the class-interval boundaries and the chart choice — that construction step is the discriminator.
checkAnswer: Interpretation: names the modal class (the interval with the highest frequency) and draws a comparative CONCLUSION about the two classes, not a single bar's value. Construction: builds a grouped frequency table with equal, non-overlapping, gap-free class intervals in clear inequality notation (e.g. 0≤t<10, 10≤t<20) so each value has exactly one class, and chooses a representation that fits the data type — touching bars/histogram or a bar chart for the grouped frequencies (a pie chart if showing proportions), NOT a line graph joining classes. Unambiguous intervals and a chart matched to the data type are the discriminating moves.
